newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices rise as Colombian strike drags on.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices rise as Colombian strike drags on.

text.p: Coffee prices rose sharply on Thursday as concern about the shortage of available supplies was heightened by an ongoing strike in Colombia.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for May delivery rose 5.45 cents to 219.75 cents a pound.
"We have a rather tight situation," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "And tightness in deliveries is being exacerbated by the Colombian situation."

A nationwide strike by the Colombian Truck Drivers' Association began at midnight on Saturday. Colombia, the second largest coffee exporter after Brazil, was hit by a portworkers strike earlier this year, a key factor in the doubling of coffee prices between December and March.
A Colombian coffee official said on Thursday that the strike could delay exports of up to 200,000 bags of coffee this week. Each bag weighs 154 pounds.
"There's an important quantity of coffee that's been held up," Diego Arango Mora, a member of the National Coffee Growers' Committee, told Reuters.
Inventories of arabica or mild South American coffee in the United States are already near historically low levels.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly futures continued to rise on growing optimism about exports. Japan recently said it was buying U.S. pork bellies to fill needs.
The U.S. bellies would replace supplies from Taiwan after an epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease on the island halted its pork exports last month.

Pork bellies for May delivery closed up the allowable 3-cent per pound daily limit at a new life-of-contract high 95.125 cents. The market has now risen about 20 cents, or more than 25 percent, in little more than a month.
Taiwan, the world's number two pork exporter last year, was shipping 16,000 metric tons of pork each month to Japan alone.
Other buyers like South Korea have also been turning to the United States to make up for the sudden loss of Taiwan pork.

The latest reports from Taiwan put 18 percent of the country's hog farms infected with the disease, with official projections that more than 3.54 million of the island's 14 million have been, or would be destroyed.
"The big thing that got that going was basically the Japanese news," said analyst Dale Durchholz of AgriVisor Services Inc.

Crude oil prices ended higher at the New York Mercantile Exchange after prices jumped late on a report that United Nations personnel were arrested by a Kurdish faction in northern Iraq with ties to Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.
U.N. officials in Iraq said they had no knowledge of the arrests. But the news jolted crude from its lacklustre trade.
Crude for June delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange settled up 30 cents at $20.03 a barrel.

A British Broadcasting Corporation report, quoting the Iraqi Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) radio, said six U.N. envoys monitoring the distribution of fuel in northern Iraq disappeared this week in areas under the control of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).
The KDP, a rival of the PUK, joined with Saddam's troops to attack PUK regions in August in northern Iraq and detained the implementation of an oil-for-food deal between the U.N. and Iraq.
The accord received final approval in December, but now dealers speculated about Hussein's connection to the KDP's alleged involvement in the arrests.
Under the deal, U.N. sanctions against Iraq were eased allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months on a renewable basis in exchange for food and other humanitarian aid.

"I think there is some concern, and it may be premature, that Saddam's possible antics may jeopardize the future of the oil-for-food sales," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst with Cargill Investor Services in New York.
May gasoline ended 1.10 cents a gallon higher at 62.84 cents a gallon and May heating oil closed up 0.24 cent a gallon at 55.89 cents.

On the Chicago Board of Trade wheat prices closed lower, weakened by forecasts for drought breaking rains in Europe and talk the recent freeze in the U.S. Great Plains may not have caused as much damage as previously anticipated.
Wheat for May delivery closed 10-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $4.21-1/2.
